title: Modal analysis of a cantilever
summary: Find the natural frequencies of a clamped-free beam and check the first one against Euler–Bernoulli — including why a finite element model always predicts frequencies that are a little too high.

steps.title: Start a Model
steps.explain: A modal analysis asks a different question from a static one — not "how far does it move under this load" but "what shapes does it like to vibrate in, and how fast". The Model is built the same way.

steps.title: Choose units
steps.explain: Millimetres for a metre-long beam. Frequencies always come back in hertz.

steps.title: Add the beam
steps.explain: A 1 m beam, 50 mm wide and 25 mm deep. The section is deliberately *not* square: a square section has the same stiffness in both bending planes, so every bending mode comes in a degenerate pair at the same frequency, which is confusing the first time you see it. A rectangle separates them.

steps.title: Density is not optional now
steps.explain: A static solve never touches `rho`; a modal solve is nothing but a fight between stiffness and mass, so `rho` is required and a Material without it makes the Step refuse. Frequencies scale as `√(E/ρ)`: get the density wrong by 10 % and every frequency is wrong by 5 %.

steps.title: Mesh it, quadratic
steps.explain: 20 elements along the beam and 2 across each section dimension, at `order: 2` (hex20). Mode shapes are curved, and a quadratic element represents curvature directly; a linear mesh needs several times as many elements for the same frequency accuracy. Giving `size` as explicit counts rather than a length puts the elements exactly where you want them.

steps.title: Clamp the root
steps.explain: A modal Step needs constraints for the same reason a static one does: without them the structure has six rigid-body modes at zero frequency, and the first real mode is the seventh. That is a legitimate analysis (it is how you check a free-floating part), but a cantilever is clamped.

steps.title: Ask for four modes
steps.explain: `procedure: "modal"` with `nModes: 4`. There are no Loads: a natural frequency is a property of the structure, not of what you do to it. The Step solves the eigenproblem `K φ = ω² M φ` — the shapes `φ` in which the elastic restoring force is exactly proportional to the inertia, so the beam can swing in them for free.

steps.title: Solve and read the frequencies
steps.explain: The Results panel lists four frequencies: about 21.1, 42.0, 131.7 and 260.3 Hz. Animate each one. Modes 1 and 3 wave in the thin direction (25 mm deep); modes 2 and 4 wave in the stiff direction (50 mm deep). The mode shapes have no magnitude — an eigenvector is only defined up to a scale factor, so the displayed amplitude means nothing and only the *shape* and the frequency are results.

steps.title: Check it against the formula, and note the sign of the error
steps.explain: Euler–Bernoulli gives 20.96, 41.91, 131.32 and 262.66 Hz. Three of the four computed values are *above* the formula, by 0.2–0.5 %. That is not a coincidence and it is worth understanding: read the theory below.
steps.theory:
For a clamped-free prismatic beam,
$$f_n = \frac{\beta_n^2}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{EI}{\rho A L^4}},\qquad \beta_1 = 1.8751,\; \beta_2 = 4.6941,\; \beta_3 = 7.8548$$
with $I = \dfrac{bh^3}{12}$ about the axis you are bending about. The $50 \times 25\,\mathrm{mm}$ section gives two different $I$, hence two interleaved families:
$21.0\,\mathrm{Hz}$ and $131\,\mathrm{Hz}$ in the thin plane, $41.9\,\mathrm{Hz}$ and $263\,\mathrm{Hz}$ in the stiff one.

**Why the computed frequencies come in from above.** A displacement finite element model can only move in the shapes its shape functions can span, so it is a *constrained* version of the real beam — and a constraint can only add stiffness, never remove it. With the consistent mass matrix (the same shape functions used for $\mathbf{M}$ as for $\mathbf{K}$) the discrete eigenvalues are therefore upper bounds on the true ones, and every frequency falls as you refine, approaching the exact value from above. If a refinement makes a frequency *rise*, look for a modelling change rather than a converging mesh.

A lumped mass matrix breaks that guarantee — it usually errs low — which is why an explicit dynamics run (which needs a lumped mass) does not give you the same bound.

**Degenerate pairs.** Give the beam a square or circular section and $I$ is the same about every axis: modes 1 and 2 then have identical frequencies, and the solver returns an arbitrary pair of shapes spanning that two-dimensional eigenspace. Two frequencies printed to five identical digits are not a bug; they are a symmetry. Any rotation of the two shapes is an equally valid answer, so never read meaning into the particular directions the solver happened to pick.

**The last mode is the least trustworthy.** Mode 4 here is $0.9\,\%$ *below* Euler–Bernoulli rather than above it, because at that wavelength the beam is no longer slender: shear deformation and rotary inertia, which the formula ignores and the solid elements include, soften the real beam. Ask for a few more modes than you need and treat the top of the list as unconverged.
